meta.ogDescription: Verified. Stephen Hawking, interviewed by Roger Highfield, The Daily Telegraph, 16 October 2001, page 1 — five weeks after 9/11. Not the 2006 or 2016 statements.

answer.sourceLine: Hawking said it in an interview with science editor Roger Highfield published in The Daily Telegraph (London) on 16 October 2001, under the headline “Colonies in space may be only hope, says Hawking.” Quote Investigator ↗ traces the line to that article down to page 1, column 3, and Wikiquote ↗ carries the same citation with the fuller passage. The popular one-sentence version is genuine — it is simply the opening sentence of a four-sentence answer.
answer.confidenceText: Verified — a real interview, a named journalist, a dated front-page article. What usually goes missing is the source, not the words.

source.excerpt: I don’t think the human race will survive the next thousand years, unless we spread into space. There are too many accidents that can befall life on a single planet. But I’m an optimist. We will reach out to the stars.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ devotes an article to this line and traces it to Roger Highfield’s interview in The Daily Telegraph of 16 October 2001, quote page 1, column 3, concluding that Hawking deserves credit for the remark.
Wikiquote ↗ lists it in its sourced Quotes section with the identical article, author and date, and preserves the two closing sentences that the popular version drops.

Hawking kept making the argument in new words: a Hong Kong news conference in June 2006 (Lawrence Journal-World ↗) and a November 2016 Oxford Union lecture (CBS News ↗) — later statements that are frequently mistaken for the source of this one.
source.excerptNote: Wikiquote ↗ gives the four-sentence passage from this interview; Quote Investigator ↗ quotes the first two sentences and supplies the page-and-column citation. The Telegraph’s own archive copy is not publicly readable, so the excerpt is reproduced from those two references rather than from a facsimile.

author.name: Stephen Hawking
author.heading: Stephen Hawking
author.bio: Stephen Hawking was a British theoretical physicist best known for his work on black holes and for A Brief History of Time (1988), the book that made him the most recognisable scientist alive. He held the Lucasian Professorship of Mathematics at Cambridge from 1979 to 2009, working for most of his career with motor neurone disease and, from the mid-1980s, a speech synthesiser. In his later decades he spent much of his public voice on risk — nuclear weapons, engineered viruses, runaway AI — and on the argument that a species confined to one planet is a species betting everything on a single throw.

misattribution.heading: It is real — the confusion is over when and where he said it
misattribution.intro: This is not a fabricated Hawking quote. The problem is the opposite: an authentic, front-page, on-the-record sentence tends to travel with no year, publication or interviewer attached. Hawking then made the same argument again in 2006 and in 2016, and those later statements are far better documented online than the 2001 interview — which makes them easy to mistake for the origin of this one.

items.why: At the Oxford Union in November 2016 Hawking said “I don’t think we will survive another 1,000 years without escaping beyond our fragile planet” (CBS News ↗). Same idea, different sentence, fifteen years later — and not the source of the line on this page.

items.who: The June 2006 Hong Kong news conference
items.why: Hawking’s widely covered 2006 Hong Kong appearance produced “It is important for the human race to spread out into space for the survival of the species” and a hundred-year framing, not a thousand-year one (Lawrence Journal-World ↗). That event is far better documented online than the 2001 Telegraph interview, which makes it easy to mistake for the source of the older quotation.

The quotation is normally cut after the first sentence, which reads as a prediction of doom. In the interview Hawking finished the thought optimistically — “But I’m an optimist. We will reach out to the stars” (Wikiquote ↗).

Plenty of lines credited to Hawking are not his. The much-shared “greatest enemy of knowledge is not ignorance, it is the illusion of knowledge” is not his either — it is usually traced to Daniel J. Boorstin, quoted saying a version of it in The Washington Post in January 1984 (New Atlas ↗). Even that is not ownership: Boorstin called the idea an aphorism rather than his own coinage, and Quote Investigator ↗ traces precursors back to Henry Thomas Buckle in 1861 while finding no direct evidence Hawking ever used the line. That background is why an unsourced Hawking quotation deserves a check — this one simply passes it.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are Hawking’s, spoken to Roger Highfield and printed on page one of The Daily Telegraph on 16 October 2001 — documented in full by Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: A front-page answer, five weeks after 9/11
lead: The interview ran on 16 October 2001, five weeks after the September 11 attacks, and Hawking used it to sort large threats from loud ones. In the same conversation he told Highfield that “Although September 11 was horrible, it didn’t threaten the survival of the human race, like nuclear weapons do” (Wikiquote ↗). The thousand-year line is the other half of that thought: the species-level risks are the ones that reach every human at once, and the only structural answer is to stop keeping every human in one place.

The quotation as it circulates stops after the first sentence, which turns a conditional argument into a doom forecast. Hawking’s full answer ends the other way round — “But I’m an optimist. We will reach out to the stars.” The clipping is what makes the quote feel like a prophecy of extinction rather than a case for spaceflight.
context.detailsSummary: Why this one keeps getting re-dated
detailsBody: Hawking made the same argument repeatedly over the following fifteen years, and the later versions are better documented online than the 2001 original — which is why the quote is so often filed under the wrong year. At a Hong Kong news conference in June 2006 he said “It is important for the human race to spread out into space for the survival of the species,” adding that Earth life faces ever-increasing risk of being wiped out by disaster (Lawrence Journal-World ↗).

In a November 2016 lecture at the Oxford Union he put it as “I don’t think we will survive another 1,000 years without escaping beyond our fragile planet” (CBS News ↗). That is a separate, later statement with its own wording — not the sentence on this page, and not its source.
context.pull: There are too many accidents that can befall life on a single planet.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator traces "I don't think the human race will survive the next thousand years, unless we spread into space" to Roger Highfield's interview in The Daily Telegraph, 16 October 2001, quote page 1, column 3, and states that Stephen Hawking deserves credit for the remark.

Wikiquote's sourced Quotes section for Stephen Hawking carries the full passage "I don't think the human race will survive the next thousand years, unless we spread into space. There are too many accidents that can befall life on a single planet. But I'm an optimist. We will reach out to the stars." cited to "Colonies in space may be only hope, says Hawking" by Roger Highfield in the Daily Telegraph (16 October 2001); the same page carries a second quotation from that interview about September 11 not threatening the survival of the human race the way nuclear weapons do.

At a November 2016 Oxford Union lecture Hawking said "I don't think we will survive another 1,000 years without escaping beyond our fragile planet" — a separate, later statement with different wording.

At a June 2006 Hong Kong news conference Hawking said "It is important for the human race to spread out into space for the survival of the species" and warned that life on Earth is at ever-increasing risk of being wiped out by disaster; the report gives moon-base, Mars and hundred-year horizons and does not mention the 2001 Daily Telegraph statement.

The "greatest enemy of knowledge is not ignorance, it is the illusion of knowledge" line often attributed to Hawking was probably Daniel J. Boorstin's, in The Washington Post in 1984; the same article quotes Hawking's June 2006 Hong Kong press-conference remarks on the risk of life on Earth being wiped out.

Quote Investigator's dedicated article on "the illusion of knowledge" finds Daniel J. Boorstin said a version of it in a January 1984 Washington Post interview, that Boorstin did not claim to originate it and labelled it an aphorism, that precursors run back to Henry Thomas Buckle's History of Civilization in England (1861), and that QI found no direct evidence Stephen Hawking used the saying.
Stephen Hawking lived 8 January 1942 – 14 March 2018, was Lucasian Professor of Mathematics at Cambridge 1979–2009, and wrote A Brief History of Time (1988).
